ae.lead: An autoencoder is trained to copy its input to its output through a layer too narrow to pass it unchanged. Nothing about that is generative — there is no distribution and no way to sample — but it established that a neural network can find a nonlinear low-dimensional code by reconstruction alone, and every latent-variable model in this lane is built on that code.

blocks.h: What PCA could and could not do
blocks.b:
Principal component analysis finds the linear subspace that captures the most variance, and it is the right answer when the data really does lie near a hyperplane. Images do not. The set of natural images is a curved, low-dimensional manifold in a very high-dimensional space, and no linear projection follows a curve.

An autoencoder replaces the linear map with an encoder network $f$ and a decoder network $g$, and minimises reconstruction error

$$\mathcal{L} = \big\| x - g(f(x)) \big\|^2$$

over a bottleneck narrower than the input. With linear layers and squared error the optimum spans the same subspace PCA finds; with nonlinearities it can bend, and Hinton and Salakhutdinov's 2006 result was that a deep one bends usefully — reconstructions from a 30-unit code that PCA at the same width could not approach.

blocks.h: Getting the deep version to train
blocks.b:
In 2006 training a deep stack by backpropagation from random initialisation did not work: gradients vanished through the layers and the optimiser settled in a poor basin. The paper's method was to pretrain the network one layer at a time as a stack of restricted Boltzmann machines, unroll the stack into an encoder and its mirror decoder, and only then fine-tune the whole thing by backpropagation.

This is the same greedy layer-wise recipe that gives the deep belief network its place in this genealogy, and the autoencoder is where it produced its most legible result. The pretraining requirement disappeared within a few years — ReLU, better initialisation and more data made deep stacks trainable directly — but the architecture it enabled did not.

blocks.h: Why it is not a generative model
blocks.b:
The bottleneck code is whatever the encoder chooses to produce. Nothing constrains its distribution: the training objective says only that the decoder must invert the encoder on the training data, so the codes may occupy an arbitrary, disconnected, oddly-shaped region of $\mathbb{R}^d$.

Sample a random $z$ and decode it and you will usually get nothing recognisable, because that $z$ is nowhere near where the encoder ever put anything. There is no density to evaluate and no procedure to sample. The autoencoder compresses; it does not model.

That gap is exactly what the VAE closes, by adding a term that pulls the code distribution towards a prior and by making the encoder output a distribution rather than a point — after which sampling from the prior and decoding is a defensible thing to do.

The encoder-bottleneck-decoder shape outlived its original purpose completely. The VAE, VQ-VAE and every latent diffusion model use it to obtain a compressed space to work in; Stable Diffusion's first stage is an autoencoder, and the diffusion happens entirely inside its latent.

The denoising variant — corrupt the input, reconstruct the original — turned out to be the more durable training signal, and it runs directly to masked autoencoders in vision and masked language modelling in NLP. Reconstruction as a self-supervised objective is the autoencoder's real bequest, and it took until the 2020s for the field to make full use of it.

refs.t: Reducing the Dimensionality of Data with Neural Networks
Extracting and Composing Robust Features with Denoising Autoencoders

vae.lead: The VAE turns the autoencoder into a probabilistic model by making the encoder output a distribution, regularising that distribution towards a prior, and — the piece that makes it trainable — rewriting the sampling step so gradients can pass through it. It is the first deep generative model with a principled objective that plain backpropagation can optimise.

blocks.b:
The quantity of interest, $\log p_\theta(x) = \log \int p_\theta(x \mid z) p(z)\, dz$, is intractable because the integral runs over every possible latent. Introducing an approximate posterior $q_\phi(z \mid x)$ gives a lower bound:

$$\log p_\theta(x) \;\geq\; \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z \mid x)}\big[\log p_\theta(x \mid z)\big] \;-\; D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(q_\phi(z \mid x) \,\|\, p(z)\big)$$

The two terms are exactly the autoencoder's two missing halves. The first is reconstruction — decode the code and match the input. The second is the regulariser the plain autoencoder lacks: it pulls each example's posterior towards the prior $\mathcal{N}(0, I)$, so the codes fill a known region rather than an arbitrary one, and sampling $z \sim p(z)$ and decoding becomes meaningful.

The gap between the bound and the true likelihood is the KL divergence between the approximate and true posteriors, which is why a more expressive $q$ gives a tighter bound — the motivation for the normalising-flow line.

The bound requires sampling $z \sim q_\phi(z \mid x)$, and one cannot backpropagate through a sampling operation: the gradient of an expectation with respect to the parameters of the distribution being sampled is not something the chain rule reaches.

The trick is to move the randomness out of the parameters. With $q_\phi$ Gaussian, write

$$z = \mu_\phi(x) + \sigma_\phi(x) \odot \epsilon, \qquad \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$$

Now $z$ is a deterministic, differentiable function of $\mu$ and $\sigma$, and $\epsilon$ is a constant as far as the gradient is concerned. The estimator that results has far lower variance than the score-function alternative, and the whole model trains with ordinary stochastic gradient descent.

The encoder is also **amortised**: one network maps any $x$ to its posterior parameters, rather than optimising a separate variational distribution per data point as classical variational inference does. That is what makes inference a single forward pass.

VAE samples are recognisable and soft. The usual explanation blames the Gaussian likelihood — a squared-error reconstruction term is the log-density of a Gaussian, and its optimum under uncertainty is the mean of the plausible outputs, which for images is a blur.

The deeper reason is that the objective is a likelihood bound. A model that assigns some probability everywhere is penalised much less for producing an unconvincing sample than for assigning near-zero probability to a real one, so the pressure is towards covering the data rather than concentrating on it. GANs make the opposite trade, which is why their samples are sharp and their coverage is not.

**Posterior collapse** is the other failure: when the decoder is powerful enough to model the data on its own, the cheapest way to minimise the KL term is to make $q_\phi(z \mid x)$ equal to the prior for every $x$, at which point the latent carries nothing. This is what VQ-VAE's discrete codes and the KL-annealing literature were written to prevent.

As a standalone image generator the VAE was overtaken quickly. As a component it is everywhere: latent diffusion runs entirely inside a VAE's latent space, and Stable Diffusion's first stage is one with an adversarial term added to sharpen it. VQ-VAE replaces the continuous latent with a discrete codebook and hands the prior to an autoregressive model, which is the route to DALL-E.

The machinery outlived the model too. The reparameterisation trick and amortised inference are standard tools well outside generative modelling, and the ELBO remains the reference objective any latent-variable model is compared against.

Stochastic Backpropagation and Approximate Inference in Deep Generative Models
beta-VAE: Learning Basic Visual Concepts with a Constrained Variational Framework

vqvae.lead: VQ-VAE replaces the VAE's continuous latent with a lookup into a learned codebook, so an image becomes a grid of integers. That removes posterior collapse by construction, and it converts generation into a problem an autoregressive model can solve — which is the shape every token-based image and audio generator since has used.

blocks.b:
The encoder produces a continuous vector at each spatial position; each is then replaced by its nearest entry in a codebook $\{e_1, \ldots, e_K\}$:

$$z_q(x) = e_k, \qquad k = \arg\min_j \big\| z_e(x) - e_j \big\|_2$$

and the decoder sees only the quantised grid. A $256 \times 256$ image might reduce to a $32 \times 32$ field of indices drawn from a vocabulary of 512 — a compression of several hundredfold that keeps enough to reconstruct the image well.

The posterior is now deterministic and one-hot, and the KL term against a uniform prior is a constant. There is no term the model can cheaply drive to zero, so the latent cannot be ignored: posterior collapse is not merely discouraged but unavailable.

Nearest-neighbour lookup has no useful gradient. VQ-VAE uses a **straight-through estimator**: the forward pass quantises, and the backward pass copies the gradient from $z_q$ to $z_e$ unchanged, as if the quantiser were the identity.

That trains the encoder and decoder but leaves the codebook itself unmoved, so two more terms are added:

$$\mathcal{L} = \underbrace{\log p(x \mid z_q(x))}_{\text{reconstruction}} + \underbrace{\big\|\mathrm{sg}[z_e(x)] - e\big\|_2^2}_{\text{codebook}} + \beta \underbrace{\big\|z_e(x) - \mathrm{sg}[e]\big\|_2^2}_{\text{commitment}}$$

where $\mathrm{sg}$ is the stop-gradient. The codebook term pulls each entry towards the encodings assigned to it; the commitment term pulls the encoder's outputs towards the codebook so they do not drift away faster than the entries can follow.

blocks.h: The prior is a separate model
blocks.b:
Quantisation alone gives compression, not generation — sampling still needs a distribution over index grids. VQ-VAE trains that separately: fit the autoencoder first, encode the dataset to index grids, then fit an autoregressive model over those grids, a PixelCNN for images and a WaveNet for audio.

The two-stage arrangement is what makes the design so portable. The autoregressive model operates on a small grid of discrete symbols rather than on raw pixels, so its quadratic or sequential costs are paid on a much shorter sequence, and any sequence model can be substituted. Replacing the PixelCNN with a Transformer is precisely what DALL-E does, with text tokens prepended so the same next-token objective handles conditioning.

The characteristic failure is that most of the codebook goes unused: a few entries win every lookup, the rest receive no gradient, and effective vocabulary shrinks far below $K$. The mitigations — exponential moving-average codebook updates, restarting dead entries, $\ell_2$-normalised codes — are standard practice rather than solved theory.

Reconstruction quality is also capped by the codebook. Fine texture that no entry represents is simply lost, which is what VQ-VAE-2's hierarchy addresses by giving layout and detail their own levels. VQGAN later added an adversarial and perceptual loss to the decoder, which sharpened reconstructions enough to make the token-based route competitive with diffusion for a period, and supplied the tokeniser that the vision-language models of the early 2020s were built on.

refs.t: Neural Discrete Representation Learning
Taming Transformers for High-Resolution Image Synthesis

vqvae2.lead: A single codebook has to encode both what the image is arranged like and what it is made of, and at any resolution one of the two suffers. VQ-VAE-2 gives them separate levels — a coarse grid for layout and a finer one for texture — with an autoregressive prior fitted to each, and reached sample quality competitive with the best GANs of its moment.

blocks.b:
The encoder produces a **top** latent at low resolution and a **bottom** latent at higher resolution, each quantised against its own codebook. The top level is decoded first and its reconstruction conditions the bottom level, so the fine grid only has to encode what the coarse one could not represent.

The division falls out of the resolutions rather than being imposed. A $32 \times 32$ grid over a $256 \times 256$ image cannot represent hair or fabric weave, so it spends its capacity on global structure; the $64 \times 64$ grid beneath it, relieved of that duty, spends its own on local detail. The paper shows the levels reconstructing exactly that split when decoded in isolation.

Sampling requires a distribution over each index grid, and the two are modelled separately. The top-level prior is a PixelCNN with self-attention layers, which it can afford because the grid is small and long-range dependencies at that resolution are what determine global coherence. The bottom-level prior is conditioned on the top level and uses a larger but purely convolutional model, since with the layout given, the remaining structure is local.

Generation runs top-down: sample a coarse grid, decode it, condition the fine prior on it, sample, and decode both together. The overall cost is far below modelling a single large grid autoregressively, because the level that needs attention is small and the level that is large does not need it.

The paper's argument is a comparison with GANs on their own ground. Likelihood-based models cover the data distribution — a mode the model cannot reach costs it likelihood — whereas an adversarial objective has no such term, and mode dropping is invisible to it.

VQ-VAE-2's samples at $256 \times 256$ and above were diverse in a way BigGAN's were not, at broadly comparable fidelity, and the paper measures it with classification-accuracy-score and precision-recall style diagnostics rather than FID alone. It is one of the clearest demonstrations that the sharpness gap between likelihood models and GANs was narrower than the field assumed, and that the diversity gap ran the other way.

The design is two models pretending to be one. The autoencoder is trained first and frozen; the priors are fitted afterwards to whatever code distribution it happened to produce. Nothing optimises the two jointly, so a codebook that is convenient for reconstruction may be hard to model autoregressively, and there is no feedback to correct that.

Sampling is also sequential and slow — thousands of forward passes to fill both grids — which is the standing cost of the autoregressive prior. And the hierarchy is fixed by hand: two levels at chosen resolutions, with a third helping at $1024 \times 1024$ and no principle saying how many there should be. Latent diffusion later took the same two-stage idea and replaced the autoregressive prior with a diffusion model over a continuous latent, which removed the sequential sampling and the codebook at once.

refs.t: Generating Diverse High-Fidelity Images with VQ-VAE-2
Neural Discrete Representation Learning

pixelcnn.lead: PixelRNN and PixelCNN model an image the way a language model models a sentence: one pixel at a time, each conditioned on all the pixels before it in a fixed raster order. The joint distribution factorises exactly, so the likelihood is tractable with no bound and no approximation — and generation costs one forward pass per pixel.

blocks.b:
Order the pixels row by row and apply the chain rule:

$$p(x) = \prod_{i=1}^{n^2} p\big(x_i \mid x_1, \ldots, x_{i-1}\big)$$

No latent variable, no bound, no adversary. Each conditional is a softmax over the 256 possible intensity values — treating intensity as categorical rather than continuous, which lets the model express multimodal conditionals such as "this pixel is either sky-blue or roof-grey" that a Gaussian output could not.

Because the likelihood is exact, these models can be compared on bits per dimension against any other density model, and they were the strongest such numbers of their moment. Colour channels are handled by extending the ordering within each pixel, so blue is conditioned on green and red as well as on all previous pixels.

blocks.h: Masked convolution, and the blind spot
blocks.b:
PixelRNN uses recurrent layers along rows and diagonals, which respects the ordering but is slow to train because the recurrence is sequential. PixelCNN instead uses convolutions with the kernel **masked** so that each position sees only pixels already generated — the centre and everything after it in raster order are zeroed out.

Masked convolutions are fully parallel at training time, since all conditionals are computed in one pass over the true image. The catch, found in the follow-up paper, is a **blind spot**: stacking masked convolutions leaves a wedge of the context above-right of each pixel that no receptive field ever reaches. Gated PixelCNN fixes it by splitting into a vertical stack that sees all rows above and a horizontal stack that sees the current row to the left, combining them so the union covers everything.

The same paper replaces ReLU with a multiplicative gate, $\tanh(W_f * x) \odot \sigma(W_g * x)$, borrowed from the LSTM and from WaveNet.

blocks.h: Fast to train, slow to sample
blocks.b:
The asymmetry is severe and structural. Training is one parallel pass; sampling is $n^2$ sequential passes, each producing a single pixel and each requiring the full network. A $256 \times 256$ image is over sixty-five thousand forward passes.

No amount of engineering removes this, because the dependency is the model. Caching intermediate activations helps by a constant factor, and later work on parallel decoding trades exactness for speed. It is the same wall autoregressive language models hit at inference, and the reason the field kept looking for models whose sampling cost does not scale with the output size.

The raster ordering itself is unnatural — it declares that a pixel depends on its neighbour above but not below, which no property of images supports — and the models are correspondingly better at texture than at global composition.

The fix was not a better ordering but a shorter sequence. VQ-VAE encodes an image to a small grid of discrete codes and fits a PixelCNN over **those**, so the autoregressive model works on a few hundred symbols rather than tens of thousands of pixels, and its weaknesses matter far less. That two-stage structure runs straight to DALL-E, which swaps the PixelCNN for a Transformer and prepends text tokens. WaveNet is the same architecture aimed at audio, where the sequential ordering is not an artefact but the truth of the signal.

refs.t: Pixel Recurrent Neural Networks
Conditional Image Generation with PixelCNN Decoders

wavenet.lead: WaveNet models raw audio one sample at a time, at sixteen thousand samples a second, using dilated causal convolutions whose receptive field grows exponentially with depth. It made synthetic speech close enough to human recordings that the gap to concatenative and parametric vocoders was widely described as halved, and it was far too slow to use as published.

blocks.b:
Causality is enforced by shifting the convolution so no output depends on a future sample. The difficulty is reach: speech has structure over hundreds of milliseconds, which at 16 kHz is thousands of samples, and a stack of ordinary convolutions would need to be thousands of layers deep.

Dilation solves it. Each layer spaces its taps out by a factor that doubles with depth — $1, 2, 4, \ldots, 512$ — and the block is repeated. Receptive field grows exponentially in depth rather than linearly, so a few tens of layers cover tens of thousands of samples.

The output is a softmax over 256 values, with the waveform companded by the $\mu$-law transform first:

$$f(x_t) = \mathrm{sign}(x_t) \, \frac{\ln(1 + \mu |x_t|)}{\ln(1 + \mu)}, \qquad \mu = 255$$

A linear 16-bit quantisation would need 65,536 softmax classes; $\mu$-law allocates resolution logarithmically, matching how loudness is perceived, and 256 classes suffice.

Each layer applies a multiplicative gate, $\tanh(W_f * x) \odot \sigma(W_g * x)$, which the paper reports clearly better than a rectifier for this signal, and the same gate appears in gated PixelCNN. Residual and skip connections run through the stack so that depth is trainable and every layer contributes to the output.

Conditioning enters in two forms. A **global** vector — speaker identity — is added to the gate's pre-activation everywhere, so one model produces many voices and switching between them is a change of one input. A **local** time series — linguistic features, or later a mel spectrogram — is upsampled to the audio rate and added the same way, which is what makes text-to-speech possible: WaveNet becomes the vocoder, and something else supplies the acoustic plan.

Generating one second of audio requires sixteen thousand sequential network evaluations. The original implementation ran orders of magnitude slower than real time, which for a text-to-speech system is not a performance issue but a disqualification.

The fixes are all about removing the sequential dependency at inference. Fast WaveNet caches the activations a dilated stack would otherwise recompute. **Parallel WaveNet** distils the trained model into an inverse-autoregressive flow that generates all samples in one pass, using a probability-density-distillation objective — this is what made the model deployable in production. Later vocoders replaced the autoregressive core entirely with flows and then with GANs.

The result that mattered beyond audio is that a fully convolutional autoregressive model can carry very long-range dependencies if the receptive field is engineered rather than left to depth. Dilated convolution became a standard primitive well outside this lane — DeepLab's atrous convolution is the same operator, aimed at spatial context instead of temporal.

The design is also the clearest statement of the autoregressive bargain: exact likelihood, stable training, no adversary and no bound, paid for with sampling cost proportional to output length. Every subsequent attempt to keep the first half and escape the second — distillation into a flow, then diffusion, then flow matching — is a response to the wall WaveNet hit.

Parallel WaveNet: Fast High-Fidelity Speech Synthesis

gan.lead: A GAN trains two networks against each other: a generator that maps noise to samples and a discriminator that tries to tell those samples from real data. There is no likelihood, no bound and no reconstruction term — the only training signal the generator receives is the discriminator's gradient, which is what makes the samples sharp and the optimisation hard.

blocks.b:
Generator $G$ and discriminator $D$ play against one value function:

$$\min_G \max_D \; V(D, G) = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_{\text{data}}}\big[\log D(x)\big] + \mathbb{E}_{z \sim p_z}\big[\log\big(1 - D(G(z))\big)\big]$$

For a fixed $G$ the optimal discriminator is $D^\star(x) = p_{\text{data}}(x) / \big(p_{\text{data}}(x) + p_g(x)\big)$, and substituting it back leaves $2 \cdot \mathrm{JSD}(p_{\text{data}} \| p_g) - \log 4$. The generator is therefore minimising the Jensen-Shannon divergence between its distribution and the data's, and the global optimum is $p_g = p_{\text{data}}$.

No term ever evaluates a density. The generator is a deterministic map from noise to samples, need not be invertible, and can concentrate probability wherever the discriminator fails to object — which is exactly why samples are sharp where likelihood-based models blur.

blocks.h: Why the stated loss is not the one used
blocks.b:
Early in training $G$ is poor, $D$ rejects its samples confidently, and $\log(1 - D(G(z)))$ is flat near zero — the generator receives almost no gradient precisely when it needs the most.

The paper's own remedy, applied in practice from the start, is to train $G$ to maximise $\log D(G(z))$ instead of minimising $\log(1 - D(G(z)))$. The fixed point is unchanged and the gradient is strong when the generator is losing. This **non-saturating** form is what every GAN implementation actually runs, and the gap between the analysed objective and the trained one is the first of several places where GAN theory and GAN practice diverge.

**Mode collapse.** Nothing in the objective rewards diversity. If the generator finds one output the discriminator cannot reject, mapping every $z$ to it is a locally excellent strategy, and the model produces one convincing image forever. A likelihood-based model cannot do this — missing a mode costs it likelihood — but an adversarial one has no corresponding term.

**Non-convergence.** The equilibrium is a saddle point of a two-player game, not a minimum of anything, so simultaneous gradient descent is not guaranteed to approach it and in practice oscillates. Worse, the JS divergence is constant wherever the two distributions have disjoint support, which for two manifolds in a high-dimensional space is the generic case — so if the discriminator becomes too good, the generator's gradient vanishes. The tension between "train $D$ to optimality, as the theory assumes" and "do not train $D$ too well, or $G$ stops learning" is unresolved in the original formulation, and it is what WGAN was written to address.

For roughly six years the GAN was the sharpest image generator available, and the line from DCGAN through PGGAN to StyleGAN is a sustained effort to make the training reliable enough to exploit that. Adversarial training also escaped generative modelling entirely: it is the loss in image-to-image translation, in domain adaptation, in the perceptual term of the autoencoders that latent diffusion depends on, and — through GAIL — in imitation learning.

What it never acquired is a usable likelihood or a stable objective, and evaluation remained proxy-based throughout. Diffusion eventually displaced it by offering comparable fidelity with a stationary training objective and no adversary, at the cost of much slower sampling.

refs.t: Generative Adversarial Networks
Improved Techniques for Training GANs

dcgan.lead: GANs worked in principle and collapsed in practice on anything larger than small greyscale digits. DCGAN is not a new objective but a set of architectural conventions — all-convolutional, batch-normalised, with specified activations — found by extensive search, that made adversarial training on natural images reliable enough for everyone else to build on.

blocks.b:
The paper's contribution is a short list, and it held for years. Replace pooling with strided convolutions in the discriminator and fractionally-strided convolutions in the generator, so the network learns its own downsampling and upsampling. Eliminate fully connected hidden layers. Apply batch normalisation in both networks, but **not** on the generator's output layer or the discriminator's input layer — normalising those was found to destabilise training. Use ReLU in the generator with $\tanh$ at the output, and LeakyReLU throughout the discriminator.

None of these is derived. They are the surviving configuration after a large empirical search, and the paper says so. Their value is that they transferred: applied to bedrooms, faces and ImageNet classes they trained without collapse, which had not previously been dependable.

blocks.h: Why the discriminator wants leaky units
blocks.b:
One rule has a legible reason. The generator's only learning signal is the gradient flowing back through the discriminator, so any part of the discriminator that zeroes its gradient is a channel through which the generator learns nothing. A plain ReLU is exactly zero below the origin, so a rejected sample lands in a region that reports no direction to move.

LeakyReLU keeps a small slope there, and the generator continues to receive a signal even where the discriminator is confidently negative. It is the same complaint that produced leaky variants in classification, made sharper because here the gradient is not merely one path among many but the entire supervision.

blocks.h: The latent space turned out to be structured
blocks.b:
The paper's more surprising result is about what the trained generator learned. Interpolating between two latent vectors produces a smooth semantic transition rather than a crossfade, which indicates the generator has learned a manifold rather than memorised examples.

More striking, vector arithmetic works: averaging the latents of several smiling women, subtracting the average of neutral women and adding the average of neutral men produces smiling men. The same structure had been observed in word embeddings, and finding it in an image generator suggested that adversarial training was recovering meaningful factors of variation rather than merely fitting a distribution. The discriminator's learned features also transferred to classification, which was the paper's argument that this was representation learning and not only synthesis.

DCGAN made GANs usable and left the underlying instability entirely intact. The objective is unchanged, the JS divergence still saturates when the two distributions have disjoint support, and mode collapse still happens — the architecture makes it less frequent, not impossible.

Because the rules are empirical, they also give no guidance beyond the regime they were found in. Scaling to higher resolution ran into fresh instabilities that no amount of following the list resolved, which is what PGGAN's growing schedule addresses. And the diagnosis of *why* training breaks had to wait for WGAN's analysis, which located the problem in the divergence rather than in the architecture.

refs.t: Unsupervised Representation Learning with Deep Convolutional Generative Adversarial Networks

wgan.lead: WGAN's contribution is a diagnosis before it is a method. The Jensen-Shannon divergence a standard GAN minimises is constant whenever the model and data distributions have disjoint support, which is the normal case — so the generator's gradient vanishes exactly when the discriminator is doing its job. Replacing it with the Wasserstein distance removes that failure at its source.

blocks.b:
Take two distributions on parallel lines a distance $\theta$ apart in the plane. The Jensen-Shannon divergence between them is $\log 2$ for every $\theta \neq 0$ and $0$ at $\theta = 0$ — a step function, with zero derivative everywhere it is defined. There is no gradient telling the generator which way to move.

This is not a contrived example. A generator maps a low-dimensional noise vector through a smooth network, so its output lies on a low-dimensional manifold; natural images do too; two such manifolds in a high-dimensional space generically fail to overlap. So the pathological case is the ordinary one, and it explains the practitioner's dilemma — a well-trained discriminator kills the generator's gradient, so the discriminator must be deliberately kept weak.

The Wasserstein or earth-mover distance behaves differently: on the same example it equals $|\theta|$, which is continuous and almost everywhere differentiable. It measures how far mass must be moved, so it is informative even when supports are disjoint.

The Wasserstein distance has a dual form usable as a loss:

$$W(\mathbb{P}_r, \mathbb{P}_g) = \sup_{\|f\|_L \leq 1} \; \mathbb{E}_{x \sim \mathbb{P}_r}\big[f(x)\big] - \mathbb{E}_{x \sim \mathbb{P}_g}\big[f(x)\big]$$

where the supremum runs over all 1-Lipschitz functions. The network that plays $f$ is called a **critic** rather than a discriminator because it is not a classifier: there is no sigmoid and no log, and its output is an unbounded score whose *difference* between real and fake is the estimate.

The consequence is that the critic can and should be trained to optimality — several critic steps per generator step, the reverse of standard GAN practice. A better critic gives a better estimate of $W$ and therefore a better gradient, which removes the balancing act the original formulation demanded.

The practical result the paper leads with is that the critic's estimate correlates with sample quality. In a standard GAN, discriminator and generator losses reflect the state of a game and can be read for nothing — a falling generator loss may mean a weakening discriminator.

With a Wasserstein critic the number is an estimate of a distance between distributions, so it falls as the model improves and can be plotted, compared across runs, and used for early stopping. Before this, GAN training was monitored by looking at samples. The paper also reports no mode collapse in its experiments, which follows from the distance being sensitive to mass the generator fails to cover.

blocks.h: Weight clipping is the weak point
blocks.b:
The Lipschitz constraint has to be enforced somehow, and WGAN's method is blunt: clamp every critic weight into $[-c, c]$ after each update. The paper is candid that this is "a terrible way" to do it.

It is a sufficient condition, not the right one. A small $c$ makes the critic nearly linear and destroys its capacity; a large $c$ makes it slow to reach the constraint boundary. Clipping also biases the critic towards very simple functions and interacts badly with batch normalisation, and the weight distribution ends up piled at the two clip values.

WGAN-GP replaces the clamp with a penalty on the gradient norm at sampled interpolation points, which enforces the same constraint far more gently and became the standard form.

refs.t: Wasserstein GAN
Towards Principled Methods for Training Generative Adversarial Networks

wgangp.lead: WGAN's analysis was right and its enforcement mechanism was not: clipping every weight into a box bounds the Lipschitz constant by destroying the critic's capacity. WGAN-GP keeps the Wasserstein objective and enforces the constraint where it is actually defined — on the gradient — by penalising deviation from unit norm at sampled points.

blocks.h: What clipping does to the critic
blocks.b:
The paper's diagnostics are the argument. With weights clamped to $[-c, c]$, the critic's weight distribution collapses onto the two boundary values, so the network is using a fraction of the function class it has parameters for. The functions it can represent become very simple — the paper shows critics that fail to capture higher moments of even toy distributions.

The gradients are also badly behaved: depending on $c$ they either vanish or explode through the layers, since clipping interacts with depth multiplicatively. Choosing $c$ is a trade between a critic too weak to be informative and one too slow to train, with no setting that avoids both.

A differentiable function is 1-Lipschitz exactly when its gradient has norm at most 1 everywhere. Rather than constrain the weights, penalise the gradient directly:

$$L = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{x} \sim \mathbb{P}_g}\big[D(\tilde{x})\big] - \mathbb{E}_{x \sim \mathbb{P}_r}\big[D(x)\big]}_{\text{Wasserstein estimate}} + \lambda \, \mathbb{E}_{\hat{x} \sim \mathbb{P}_{\hat{x}}}\Big[\big(\|\nabla_{\hat{x}} D(\hat{x})\|_2 - 1\big)^2\Big]$$

with $\lambda = 10$ throughout the paper. The penalty is two-sided — it pushes the norm towards exactly 1, not merely below it — because the optimal critic under the dual has unit gradient norm almost everywhere along the transport paths.

The points $\hat{x}$ are sampled along straight lines between real and generated samples, since it is the region between the two distributions where the critic's slope determines the generator's gradient, and enforcing the constraint over the whole input space is neither tractable nor necessary.

A consequence that is easy to miss: the penalty constrains the gradient of the critic's output **with respect to a single input**, and batch normalisation makes the output of one example depend on the others in its batch. The quantity being penalised is then not the one the theory refers to.

So batch normalisation is removed from the critic, and layer normalisation is suggested in its place. The generator keeps it. This is one of the clearer cases in the lane where a training technique had to be dropped because it violated an assumption of the objective rather than because it performed badly.

blocks.h: What it enabled, and what it costs
blocks.b:
The paper's headline is robustness: the same hyperparameters train a wide range of architectures, including a deep residual generator and a 101-layer critic, and a character-level language model over discrete data — configurations that standard GAN objectives failed on. That reliability is what made the deeper, higher-resolution GAN work of the following years feasible, and PGGAN builds directly on it.

The costs are two. The penalty requires a gradient of a gradient, so each critic step needs a double backward pass and costs meaningfully more time and memory. And the constraint is enforced only where it is sampled — along interpolation lines — so it is a soft, local approximation of a global condition, and nothing guarantees the critic is Lipschitz elsewhere. Spectral normalisation later offered a cheaper route by bounding each layer's spectral norm directly, and BigGAN uses that rather than the penalty.

refs.t: Improved Training of Wasserstein GANs
Wasserstein GAN
Spectral Normalization for Generative Adversarial Networks

pggan.lead: High-resolution GAN training failed early and for a compounding reason: at $1024^2$ the discriminator can separate real from fake almost immediately, gradients become useless, and the memory required forces batches too small to be stable. PGGAN's answer is a curriculum — start at $4 \times 4$ and add a layer pair at a time, fading each in smoothly.

blocks.b:
Training begins with a generator and discriminator that operate at $4 \times 4$. Once that converges, a new block is added to each — the generator gains an upsampling stage, the discriminator a downsampling one — and training continues at $8 \times 8$, and so on to $1024 \times 1024$.

The new layers are **faded in** rather than switched on. A weight $\alpha$ moves from 0 to 1 over many iterations, linearly interpolating between the upsampled output of the existing network and the output of the new block, so the previously trained layers never receive a sudden shock.

The curriculum is doing two things. It lets the networks settle global structure at a resolution where the problem is easy before any fine detail is asked for, and it means most of training happens at low resolution, where iterations are cheap — the paper reports a substantial speedup over training at full resolution throughout.

**Minibatch standard deviation.** A layer near the end of the discriminator computes the standard deviation of each feature across the batch, averages it, and appends it as an extra feature map. The discriminator can then detect a generator whose outputs are all alike, which gives mode collapse a direct cost — a rare instance of diversity entering an adversarial objective explicitly.

**Equalised learning rate.** Weights are initialised from a unit normal and scaled at runtime by the He constant, so every layer's effective learning rate is the same. With Adam's per-parameter normalisation, layers with different weight scales otherwise train at different speeds.

**Pixelwise feature normalisation.** In the generator, each position's feature vector is normalised to unit length after every convolution. It prevents the escalating magnitudes that appear when the two networks compete, and does the job batch normalisation would without the batch dependence.

There was no face dataset at $1024^2$, so the paper built CelebA-HQ by selecting and upscaling 30,000 images from CelebA with a careful filtering and super-resolution pipeline. The result became the standard benchmark for high-resolution generation and the substrate for StyleGAN's development, and it is a reminder that this line of work was gated on data as much as on method.

The paper also proposes a sliced-Wasserstein-distance metric over local image patches at multiple scales, on the argument that FID and Inception score are insensitive to the fine texture failures that matter at this resolution.

Nothing about the adversarial game changes. PGGAN is a training procedure — an ordering of the problem — layered on top of WGAN-GP, and its stabilisers treat symptoms individually rather than following from any analysis.

The schedule brings its own complexity: how long to train at each resolution and how quickly to fade are hyperparameters with no principle behind them, and the whole run is a sequence of phases rather than a single optimisation. StyleGAN2 later found that progressive growing leaves a specific artefact — a preference for features to stick to particular pixel coordinates, because each resolution is trained to produce a complete output on its own — and removed the growing entirely in favour of a skip-connected architecture that trains at full resolution from the start.

refs.t: Progressive Growing of GANs for Improved Quality, Stability, and Variation

stylegan.lead: A conventional GAN generator takes a latent vector at the input and everything downstream is determined by it, which gives no handle on any particular aspect of the output. StyleGAN restructures the generator so the latent enters at every layer as a **style**, and the resolution at which it enters decides what it controls.

blocks.b:
The input latent $z$ is drawn from a fixed Gaussian, which forces the generator to warp a spherical distribution onto whatever shape the data occupies. Where a factor is absent from the training set — the combination of features that never co-occur — that warping becomes highly curved, which is what makes interpolation in $z$ produce implausible intermediates.

StyleGAN inserts an eight-layer MLP mapping $z$ to an intermediate space $\mathcal{W}$, which is not required to follow any fixed distribution and can therefore be **disentangled** — the paper introduces perceptual path length and linear separability to measure this, and shows $\mathcal{W}$ scoring far better than $\mathcal{Z}$ on both.

The synthesis network then starts from a learned constant $4 \times 4 \times 512$ tensor. The latent no longer enters at the input at all.

blocks.h: AdaIN, and where in the stack a style acts
blocks.b:
$w \in \mathcal{W}$ is projected per layer into a scale and bias, and applied by adaptive instance normalisation:

$$\mathrm{AdaIN}(x_i, y) = y_{s,i} \, \frac{x_i - \mu(x_i)}{\sigma(x_i)} + y_{b,i}$$

Normalising each feature map to zero mean and unit variance erases the previous style before the new one is applied, so each layer's style controls that layer and does not accumulate.

Because layers operate at different resolutions, the styles separate by scale on their own. Coarse layers control pose and face shape; middle layers hair style and expression; fine layers colour and micro-texture. **Style mixing** — feeding one $w$ to the coarse layers and another to the fine ones — makes the split visible and is used during training as a regulariser that discourages adjacent layers from correlating.

Per-pixel Gaussian **noise** is added at every layer for stochastic detail — the exact placement of hairs or pores — which frees the latent from having to encode variation nobody wants control over.

Sampling from the tail of the latent distribution gives poorly-modelled outputs, since those regions are rare in training. Truncation shrinks samples towards the mean, $w' = \bar{w} + \psi(w - \bar{w})$ with $\psi < 1$, trading variety for fidelity.

Doing this in $\mathcal{W}$ rather than $\mathcal{Z}$ is what makes it work well: the mean of a disentangled space is an average face, and moving towards it degrades gracefully, whereas the same operation in $\mathcal{Z}$ passes through the distorted regions the mapping network was introduced to avoid. Truncation can also be applied only to the coarse layers, keeping fine detail varied.

StyleGAN's outputs contain a characteristic droplet-shaped artefact, visible in feature maps from $64 \times 64$ upward and sometimes in the final image. StyleGAN2's diagnosis is that it is caused by AdaIN itself: normalising away the mean and variance of each feature map destroys information carried in those statistics, and the generator learns to smuggle it past by creating a strong localised spike that dominates the statistic.

The architecture also inherits progressive growing from PGGAN, and with it a second artefact — details that stay fixed to pixel coordinates rather than moving with the face, because each resolution was trained to output a complete image. Both are removed in the successor: weight demodulation replaces AdaIN, and a skip-connected design replaces growing.

The model remains, like every GAN in this lane, one model per domain with no likelihood and no inference path — projecting a real image back into $\mathcal{W}$ requires a separate optimisation, which is what the GAN-inversion literature exists to do.

refs.t: A Style-Based Generator Architecture for Generative Adversarial Networks
Arbitrary Style Transfer in Real-time with Adaptive Instance Normalization

stylegan2.lead: StyleGAN produced the best faces available and two signature defects: blob artefacts traceable to AdaIN, and detail that clung to pixel coordinates instead of moving with the subject. StyleGAN2 removes the first by replacing normalisation with weight demodulation; StyleGAN3 removes the second by treating the generator as a continuous signal and fixing its sampling.

blocks.b:
AdaIN normalises the actual feature statistics of each map, which discards information the generator wants and provokes it to create a dominating spike to preserve that information past the normalisation — the droplet.

StyleGAN2 removes the operation from the activations and folds it into the weights. Modulation scales the convolution weights by the style, $w'_{ijk} = s_i \cdot w_{ijk}$, and demodulation then rescales by the expected output standard deviation:

$$w''_{ijk} = \frac{w'_{ijk}}{\sqrt{\sum_{i,k} {w'_{ijk}}^2 + \epsilon}}$$

This normalises on the *assumption* of unit-variance inputs rather than on measured statistics, so it is a deterministic operation on the weights alone. The blobs disappear completely, and the operation is cheaper than AdaIN because it touches weights rather than activations.

blocks.h: No more growing, and a smoother latent map
blocks.b:
Progressive growing is dropped. Each resolution in PGGAN's schedule is briefly trained to produce a finished image on its own, which teaches it to place high-frequency detail at fixed positions — the source of the sticking. StyleGAN2 trains at full resolution throughout, using skip connections in the generator and residual connections in the discriminator to keep the deep stack trainable, and reports better results without any curriculum.

**Path length regularisation** is added: a penalty encouraging a fixed-size step in $\mathcal{W}$ to produce a fixed-magnitude change in the image, regardless of direction. It makes the generator's mapping better conditioned, which improves sample quality and — usefully — makes projecting a real image back into $\mathcal{W}$ far more reliable. Both this and the $R_1$ gradient penalty are applied **lazily**, once every several minibatches, since the paper finds no loss from doing so and a clear saving.

The remaining defect is subtler: translating the latent should translate the image, and in StyleGAN2 it does not — textures drift relative to the face, an effect visible in video and known as texture sticking.

The diagnosis is signal processing. The generator's nonlinearities produce frequencies above the Nyquist limit of the feature grid, and those alias — they fold down and become locked to the pixel lattice rather than to the underlying content. StyleGAN3 treats every feature map as a regularly sampled continuous signal and makes each operation alias-free: low-pass filters around the nonlinearities, careful upsampling filters, and Fourier features rather than a learned constant as the input.

The result is a generator equivariant to translation and rotation, in which detail moves with the subject. It is markedly better for video and animation, and slightly worse on FID — the artefacts it removes were, in still-image metrics, partly helping.

StyleGAN2 and 3 remain the reference for high-fidelity face and single-domain generation, and their latent space is more useful for editing than anything diffusion offered for years: directions in $\mathcal{W}$ correspond to interpretable attributes, and the inversion tooling built around it made real-image editing practical.

The constraints are the family's. One model per domain, trained on a curated dataset; no likelihood; no text conditioning; and training that costs thousands of GPU-hours and can still fail. Text-conditioned diffusion arrived with none of the fidelity advantage on faces but with generality across every domain at once, and that is what ended the line's dominance rather than any defect these papers left unfixed.

refs.t: Analyzing and Improving the Image Quality of StyleGAN
Alias-Free Generative Adversarial Networks

biggan.lead: The GAN literature had improved objectives and architectures without ever asking what happened at the scale classifiers were being trained at. BigGAN answers that question directly — larger batches, wider layers, and the engineering needed to keep the training alive — and finds most of the gain sitting in plain scale, along with a new failure mode.

blocks.b:
The paper's opening result is that increasing the batch size to 2048 improves the Inception score substantially, and that widening every layer by half again adds more. Both are reported as straightforward gains from more compute per step, with no change to the objective.

The reading offered is that a larger batch covers more modes per update, so the gradient is a better estimate of the true one and the generator's diversity improves. The paper is also frank about the other consequence: larger batches reach a good state faster and then become unstable, so the models reach their best score before collapsing rather than converging.

Conditioning is threaded through the whole generator rather than concatenated once. Class-conditional batch normalisation supplies each layer's normalisation gain and bias from a **shared** class embedding, and the noise vector is split into chunks that are fed to different resolutions — a hierarchical latent, so the same $z$ influences coarse and fine structure through separate paths.

Sharing one embedding across layers rather than learning a separate one per layer cuts parameters and, the paper reports, improves training speed. The discriminator uses projection conditioning, taking an inner product between the class embedding and its feature vector, and both networks use spectral normalisation to bound their Lipschitz constants — cheaper than WGAN-GP's double backward pass and, at this scale, the practical choice.

The most-copied idea in the paper is at sampling time. Train with $z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$, but sample with values whose magnitude exceeds a threshold resampled — a truncated normal. Shrinking the threshold moves samples towards the mode of the latent distribution.

This exposes the fidelity-variety trade as a dial that can be turned **after** training rather than a property fixed by it: a single model produces a whole curve of operating points, and Inception score and FID move in opposite directions along it. Very large models saturate — heavy truncation produces artefacts rather than cleaner samples — and orthogonal regularisation on the generator's weights is applied to make them better behaved under truncation.

The idea generalised well beyond GANs; classifier-free guidance in diffusion is the same manoeuvre, trading diversity for fidelity at inference.

BigGAN's training collapses, reliably, late in the run. The paper's analysis is unusually thorough: it tracks the top singular values of the weight matrices in both networks and finds the generator's growing without bound, with collapse coinciding with the discriminator's spectra behaving sharply.

Several interventions were tried — constraining the generator's spectra directly, various penalties — and each delayed collapse at a cost in sample quality; none prevented it. The paper's conclusion is that stability comes from the interaction of the two networks rather than from either alone, and that enforcing it on one side is possible but not free. The practical method is early stopping.

This is where the adversarial line's honesty is clearest: after five years of stabilisation work, the strongest GAN available still had to be stopped before it destroyed itself, and mode dropping remained detectable on ImageNet. Diffusion models arrived with a stationary regression objective that has no such dynamics, and that — more than fidelity — is what moved the field.

refs.t: Large Scale GAN Training for High Fidelity Natural Image Synthesis
Spectral Normalization for Generative Adversarial Networks
cGANs with Projection Discriminator

cgan.lead: A GAN samples from the data distribution and offers no say over what it produces. The conditional GAN adds an input $y$ to both networks — the generator makes a sample given $y$, the discriminator judges whether the pair is real — which converts an unconditional sampler into a controllable one with almost no change to the objective.

blocks.b:
The minimax game gains one argument throughout:

$$\min_G \max_D \; \mathbb{E}_{x, y}\big[\log D(x \mid y)\big] + \mathbb{E}_{z, y}\big[\log\big(1 - D(G(z \mid y) \mid y)\big)\big]$$

That the **discriminator** is conditioned as well is the essential detail. If only the generator saw $y$, the discriminator could not tell a realistic image paired with the wrong label from a correctly paired one, so nothing would penalise ignoring the condition. Judging the pair is what makes $y$ binding.

In the original paper both are fed the label by concatenating a one-hot vector to their inputs — the simplest possible mechanism, on MNIST digits and on a multi-label image tagging task.

The generator is free to disregard $y$ wherever doing so is easier, and the only force against that is the discriminator's ability to notice. When the discriminator is weak on the conditional relationship — because $y$ is high-dimensional, or because the pairing is subtle — the generator drifts towards producing plausible outputs unrelated to the input.

This shows up sharply in text-to-image work, where a model produces a beautiful image that ignores half the prompt. The remedies are all about strengthening the conditional signal: projection discriminators that take an inner product with the class embedding rather than concatenating it, auxiliary classifier losses, and — in diffusion — classifier-free guidance, which extrapolates away from the unconditional prediction to force conditioning to bite.

Concatenation at the input is weak because the signal dilutes as it passes through the network. Later work moved conditioning into the normalisation layers instead — conditional batch normalisation supplies a per-class gain and bias at every layer, which is how BigGAN conditions, and StyleGAN's AdaIN is the same mechanism used for an unlabelled style vector.

The general lesson travelled well past GANs. Diffusion models condition through cross-attention or adaptive normalisation rather than concatenation, and DiT's ablation finds adaptive layer norm clearly the best of the options it tests. Conditioning is an architectural question, not merely an extra input.

The conditional formulation is what makes the adversarial family useful rather than merely interesting. Class-conditional generation, image-to-image translation, super-resolution, inpainting and text-to-image are all instances of it, and pix2pix is the moment it became a general recipe rather than a per-task design.

The paper itself is short and its experiments are modest — a two-page workshop-style note in 2014, with MNIST digits conditioned on labels. Its importance is entirely in what the formulation allowed afterwards, which is a common shape in this lane.

refs.t: Conditional Generative Adversarial Nets
cGANs with Projection Discriminator

pix2pix.lead: Image-to-image problems — sketch to photo, map to aerial, labels to scene — had each been solved with a bespoke loss encoding what mattered for that pairing. pix2pix replaces the hand-designed term with a conditional discriminator that learns what "looks correct" means for the task, and the same architecture then handles all of them.

blocks.b:
Train a network to map input to output under squared error and it produces the conditional mean. Where the mapping is genuinely ambiguous — many photographs are consistent with one sketch — the mean of the plausible outputs is not a plausible output, and the result is blurred.

A discriminator has no such tendency. It is trained to reject anything that does not look like a real image, and the average of several plausible images is easy to reject. So the adversarial term supplies exactly the thing a per-pixel loss cannot: a learned notion of which outputs are admissible.

The two are combined rather than substituted. The full objective keeps an $L_1$ term alongside the adversarial one:

$$G^\star = \arg\min_G \max_D \; \mathcal{L}_{\text{cGAN}}(G, D) + \lambda \, \mathcal{L}_{L_1}(G)$$

with $\lambda = 100$. The $L_1$ term keeps the output near the ground truth at low frequencies; the discriminator handles the high frequencies where blur would otherwise appear. $L_1$ rather than $L_2$ because it blurs less.

Since $L_1$ already enforces low-frequency correctness, the discriminator only needs to police local realism. pix2pix therefore uses a **PatchGAN**: a fully convolutional discriminator that classifies each $N \times N$ patch of the image and averages the responses.

The consequences are practical. The discriminator has far fewer parameters, runs faster, and applies to images of any size, since it is convolutional. The paper's ablation over patch size finds $70 \times 70$ a good setting — smaller patches give tiling artefacts, and a full-image discriminator gives no improvement over the patch version at higher cost.

The generator is a U-Net. For these tasks the input and output share structure — edges in a sketch become edges in a photograph — and skip connections let that structure pass directly from encoder to decoder rather than being squeezed through a bottleneck and reconstructed.

A conditional GAN should map $(z, x)$ to a distribution over outputs, and pix2pix does not: the paper reports that the generator learns to ignore the noise input entirely, so the mapping is effectively deterministic. Dropout at training and test time is used to inject some stochasticity, and the resulting variation is minor.

The reason is that the strong $L_1$ term rewards matching the one ground-truth output, which makes any use of $z$ a liability. So the model produces one output per input — fine for tasks with a single right answer, wrong for genuinely one-to-many mappings. BicycleGAN was written specifically to recover the diversity, by enforcing an invertible relationship between the latent and the output.

Training requires aligned pairs: the same scene as a label map and as a photograph, pixel for pixel. For some tasks that is free — edges can be extracted automatically, colour can be desaturated — and for others it is prohibitive. There is no dataset of the same horse as a zebra.

CycleGAN removes exactly this requirement by replacing the pairing with a cycle-consistency constraint over two unpaired collections, which is the single most consequential extension of pix2pix's setup. The framework also inherits everything adversarial training carries: no likelihood, unstable optimisation, and evaluation that ends up leaning on human judgement — the paper runs perceptual studies on Mechanical Turk and a "FCN-score" using an off-the-shelf segmenter, both proxies.

refs.t: Image-to-Image Translation with Conditional Adversarial Networks
Toward Multimodal Image-to-Image Translation

cyclegan.lead: pix2pix needs the same scene photographed twice, once in each domain, and for most interesting translations that data does not exist. CycleGAN drops the pairing entirely and constrains the problem a different way: translate to the other domain and back, and require that you arrive where you started.

blocks.h: Why an adversarial loss alone is not enough
blocks.b:
With two unpaired collections, one can train $G : X \to Y$ so that its outputs fool a discriminator on $Y$. That constrains the *distribution* of outputs and says nothing about the correspondence: any permutation of the target domain satisfies it equally well, so a photograph of a particular horse may become a zebra that has nothing to do with it.

The problem is under-determined, and the adversarial term cannot determine it. CycleGAN adds an assumption — that the translation should be invertible — and trains a second generator $F : Y \to X$ to enforce it:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{cyc}}(G, F) = \mathbb{E}_{x}\big[\|F(G(x)) - x\|_1\big] + \mathbb{E}_{y}\big[\|G(F(y)) - y\|_1\big]$$

A translation that discards the input's content cannot be inverted, so the cycle term penalises exactly the failure the adversarial loss admits. Four networks are trained together: two generators and two discriminators.

The adversarial term uses a least-squares form rather than the log-likelihood one — LSGAN — which the paper finds more stable and which gives better-behaved gradients for the generator. Discriminators are updated against a buffer of previously generated images rather than only the current batch, which damps oscillation between the two networks.

An **identity loss** is added for tasks where colour should be preserved: feeding a target-domain image to the generator that maps into that domain should return it unchanged. Without it the paper observes hue shifts in photograph-to-painting translation.

The generators are residual convolutional networks and the discriminators are PatchGANs, both inherited from pix2pix and from the neural style transfer literature.

The constraint is weaker than it looks. Later analysis showed CycleGAN generators learning to hide information about the input in imperceptible high-frequency patterns, so the reverse generator can recover the original without the forward translation having genuinely preserved the content — a steganographic solution that satisfies the loss while defeating its purpose.

The assumption is also substantive and often wrong. Invertibility asserts a bijection between the domains, so translations that must add or remove information — a summer photograph to a snow-covered one, where the snow's exact form is not determined — are outside what the constraint can express. In practice CycleGAN is strong on texture and colour changes and weak on geometry: horses become zebras reliably, dogs do not become cats.

The paper's importance is as an existence proof that a learned correspondence can be recovered from two unpaired collections with a structural constraint alone, and the results — horses and zebras, summer and winter, Monet and photographs — became among the most widely reproduced images in the field.

The cycle idea generalised well beyond images: unsupervised machine translation uses back-translation on precisely this logic, and unpaired domain adaptation borrows it directly. Its own line was largely closed out by conditional diffusion and by large text-conditioned models, which perform the same translations from a text description without needing a second domain collection at all.

refs.t: Unpaired Image-to-Image Translation using Cycle-Consistent Adversarial Networks
CycleGAN, a Master of Steganography

nice.lead: The VAE optimises a bound on the likelihood because the exact one is intractable. NICE asks what class of models makes it tractable, and answers: those built from invertible transformations whose Jacobian determinant is trivial to compute. Its coupling layer is the construction that makes that possible, and every normalising flow since is a variation on it.

blocks.b:
If $z = f(x)$ is invertible, the density of $x$ follows exactly:

$$\log p_X(x) = \log p_Z(f(x)) + \log\left|\det \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right|$$

So an exact likelihood is available with no bound and no adversary — provided the determinant can be computed. For a general $D \times D$ Jacobian that costs $O(D^3)$, which for images is out of the question, and the whole design problem is finding invertible maps whose determinant is cheap.

NICE's answer is to split the input in two and transform only one half using the other:

$$y_{1:d} = x_{1:d}, \qquad y_{d+1:D} = x_{d+1:D} + m(x_{1:d})$$

The Jacobian is lower triangular with ones on the diagonal, so its determinant is exactly 1 — the transformation is **volume-preserving**. The inverse requires no inversion of $m$: recover $x_{1:d}$ directly, evaluate $m$ on it, subtract. So $m$ can be an arbitrarily complicated neural network, and both directions cost one forward pass.

The untouched half is the price, and the fix is to alternate which half is which across layers. Three or four coupling layers suffice for every dimension to have influenced every other.

A stack of volume-preserving maps cannot change total volume, so the model cannot allocate more density to some directions than others. NICE adds a final diagonal scaling layer, $z_i = s_i \, y_i$, whose log-determinant is $\sum_i \log |s_i|$.

The learned $s_i$ then act as a measure of importance per latent dimension — small $s_i$ means that direction carries little variation, which the paper notes gives something analogous to the spectrum in PCA. It is a small addition that turns a rigid map into one that can decide where the data actually lives.

blocks.h: Where flows are strong and weak
blocks.b:
The bargain is unusual: exact likelihood, exact inference in one pass, and sampling in one pass, all from the same network run in opposite directions. No other family in this lane offers all three, and no bound is ever taken.

The cost is structural. Invertibility forces the latent space to have exactly the dimension of the data, so there is no compression, and every layer must be invertible, which rules out most of the architectural vocabulary the rest of the field uses. The volume-preserving constraint is loosened by RealNVP's affine coupling, which introduces a learned scale as well as a shift; Glow generalises the fixed alternation into a learned invertible $1 \times 1$ convolution; and the continuous-time line replaces the layer stack with an ODE. Sample quality nevertheless remained behind GANs and later diffusion throughout, which is the standing verdict on the family.

refs.t: NICE: Non-linear Independent Components Estimation
Variational Inference with Normalizing Flows

realnvp.lead: NICE's coupling layers can only shift, never scale, so the whole transformation preserves volume and the model cannot concentrate density. RealNVP's affine coupling adds a learned scale alongside the shift, keeping the triangular Jacobian, and pairs it with a multi-scale architecture that makes the family workable on natural images.

blocks.b:
The transformed half gains a multiplicative term:

$$y_{1:d} = x_{1:d}, \qquad y_{d+1:D} = x_{d+1:D} \odot \exp\big(s(x_{1:d})\big) + t(x_{1:d})$$

The Jacobian is still triangular, so the log-determinant is just the sum of the scale outputs, $\sum_j s_j(x_{1:d})$ — computed for free from a quantity the layer already produced. Inversion remains explicit and needs no inversion of $s$ or $t$, so both can be arbitrary networks.

What the scale buys is the ability to expand and contract volume locally, which is what lets the model place high density on the data manifold and low density elsewhere. NICE could only translate probability mass around; RealNVP can concentrate it.

For images the split is done by masking rather than by slicing a vector. Two patterns alternate: a **checkerboard** mask, which conditions on alternating pixels and captures local structure, and a **channel-wise** mask applied after a squeeze operation that trades spatial resolution for channel depth, which captures structure across channels.

Alternating the two, and alternating which side of each mask is transformed, is what gives every dimension influence over every other within a modest number of layers. The squeeze operation — reshaping a $4 \times 4 \times c$ block into $2 \times 2 \times 4c$ — is what makes the channel-wise masking meaningful, since it folds spatial neighbours into channels.

The architecture is a hierarchy. After a few coupling layers at one scale, half the dimensions are **factored out** — sent directly to the latent and not processed further — and the rest continue into the next scale.

This does two things. It reduces the computational and memory cost substantially, since later layers operate on fewer dimensions. And it distributes the latent across scales, so some dimensions capture fine local detail and others global structure, which the paper shows by resampling one level while holding the others fixed.

The practical consequence is that RealNVP was the first flow to produce recognisable samples on CelebA, LSUN and ImageNet at $32 \times 32$ and $64 \times 64$, and to report competitive bits-per-dimension against autoregressive models — while sampling in a single pass rather than pixel by pixel.

The samples are recognisable and clearly inferior to GAN output of the same period, and this is characteristic of the family rather than a tuning failure. A likelihood objective spreads mass to cover the data, and an invertible architecture is far more constrained than an unconstrained decoder, so the model spends capacity on being invertible rather than on being expressive.

Dimensionality is the harder constraint: the latent must match the data exactly, so a $256 \times 256 \times 3$ image needs almost two hundred thousand latent dimensions. There is no compression, and memory scales accordingly.

The fixed alternating masks are also arbitrary — nothing says a checkerboard is the right partition — which is precisely what Glow replaces with a learned invertible $1 \times 1$ convolution, a general linear mixing of channels whose determinant is still cheap.

refs.t: Density estimation using Real NVP
NICE: Non-linear Independent Components Estimation

maf.lead: Coupling layers leave half their input untouched at every step, which is what makes them cheap and what limits them. Autoregressive flows transform every dimension at once, conditioning each on all the previous ones — the Jacobian is still triangular — and the resulting pair, MAF and IAF, are exact inverses of each other with opposite performance profiles.

blocks.b:
Write each dimension as a location-scale transform of a noise variable, conditioned on everything before it:

$$x_i = u_i \exp(\alpha_i) + \mu_i, \qquad \mu_i = f_{\mu}(x_{1:i-1}), \; \alpha_i = f_{\alpha}(x_{1:i-1})$$

Because $\mu_i$ and $\alpha_i$ depend only on earlier dimensions, the Jacobian is triangular and its log-determinant is $-\sum_i \alpha_i$. This is the same trick coupling layers use, taken to its limit: instead of one split, a chain of $D$ nested conditionings.

The conditioners are computed in one pass by a MADE network — a masked autoencoder whose weight masks enforce the ordering — so training does not require $D$ separate evaluations.

blocks.h: MAF and IAF are the same layer, run backwards
blocks.b:
**MAF** parameterises the map from data to noise. Evaluating a density is one parallel pass, because all the conditioners depend on $x$, which is given. Sampling requires generating $x_1$, then $x_2$ from it, and so on — $D$ sequential passes.

**IAF** parameterises the map from noise to data, conditioning each $x_i$ on $u_{1:i-1}$. Now sampling is one parallel pass and density evaluation of an external point is sequential.

So the two have exactly reversed costs, and the choice is dictated by use. IAF is what you want inside a VAE, as a flexible posterior that must be sampled from cheaply; MAF is what you want as a density estimator for data you already hold. The paper makes this correspondence explicit — MAF and IAF are the same model viewed in opposite directions, and RealNVP is the special case where the conditioning is a single split rather than a full chain.

blocks.h: Fast density or fast sampling, never both
blocks.b:
The asymmetry is not an implementation problem; it is the structure of the model. One direction is parallel because its conditioners depend on quantities that are all available, and the other is sequential because they are not.

The resolution the field found is to train one and distil into the other. **Parallel WaveNet** trains an autoregressive WaveNet as a teacher and distils it into an IAF student using a probability-density-distillation objective — the student can be sampled in one pass, the teacher can score, and the training only ever needs the direction each is good at. That construction is what made WaveNet deployable, and it is the clearest practical consequence of this arrow.

Autoregressive flows inherit the awkwardness of an arbitrary variable ordering: for images the raster order asserts dependencies that the data does not have. Stacking layers with different orderings helps and does not remove the underlying arbitrariness.

As density estimators MAF was strong — competitive bits-per-dimension on tabular data and images at the time — and as image generators the whole flow family remained behind GANs, for the reasons the invertibility constraint imposes. The line's more durable contribution is conceptual: it made explicit that autoregressive models, coupling flows and normalising flows are one family distinguished by how much of the input each step is allowed to see, which is the framing the continuous-time flows then generalised.

MADE: Masked Autoencoder for Distribution Estimation

glow.lead: RealNVP alternates fixed masks to decide which dimensions mix, which is arbitrary and limits how information can flow between channels. Glow replaces the fixed permutation with a learned invertible $1 \times 1$ convolution — a general linear mixing whose determinant is still cheap — and produced the first flow samples of genuinely high quality.

blocks.b:
Between coupling layers RealNVP reverses or shuffles the channel order so that different dimensions are transformed each time. A permutation is a special case of an invertible linear map; Glow simply learns the general one.

A $1 \times 1$ convolution with $c$ input and output channels applies a $c \times c$ matrix $W$ at every spatial position. For an $h \times w$ feature map the log-determinant is

$$\log\left|\det \frac{\partial \, \mathrm{conv}(h; W)}{\partial h}\right| = h \cdot w \cdot \log|\det W|$$

so the cost is one $c \times c$ determinant, negligible next to the convolutions around it. Parameterising $W$ by its LU decomposition reduces that to a product of diagonal entries and makes the determinant $O(c)$, with invertibility guaranteed by construction rather than hoped for.

Batch normalisation is unusable here: it makes each example's output depend on its batch, which breaks the invertibility the change-of-variables formula requires, and it is noisy at the small batch sizes large flows need.

**Actnorm** replaces it — a per-channel scale and bias, initialised from the first minibatch so that its output has zero mean and unit variance, and then trained as ordinary parameters. It is data-dependent initialisation rather than normalisation, so it is invertible and batch-independent.

The Glow block is then three steps repeated: actnorm, invertible $1 \times 1$ convolution, affine coupling, arranged in RealNVP's multi-scale hierarchy with squeezing and factoring out.

blocks.h: Manipulation in a latent that means something
blocks.b:
Because the model is exactly invertible, any image can be encoded to its latent in one pass — no optimisation, unlike GAN inversion. The paper exploits this: encode a set of images with an attribute and a set without, take the difference of the means, and adding that vector to any image's latent applies the attribute.

Smiling, age, hair colour and beard are all manipulated this way on $256 \times 256$ faces, and interpolation between two real images is a straight line in latent space decoded back. Temperature-scaled sampling — drawing from $\mathcal{N}(0, T^2)$ with $T$ below 1 — trades diversity for fidelity, the same manoeuvre as BigGAN's truncation.

Exact encoding for real images is something no GAN of the period could do, and it is the flow family's clearest practical advantage.

Glow's samples are the best the flow line produced and still below contemporary GANs, and the model is enormous for what it delivers: the reported face model runs to hundreds of millions of parameters and took a large multi-GPU budget for images GANs were producing more cheaply.

The reason is the standing constraint. Latent dimension equals data dimension, so there is no compression anywhere in the model, and every layer must be invertible, which excludes most of the architectural vocabulary available elsewhere. Depth is the only way to buy expressiveness, and depth in an invertible network is expensive in both parameters and memory.

The line's response was to stop insisting on discrete invertible layers. Neural ODEs make the transformation continuous, which replaces the determinant with a trace, and FFJORD then removes the structural constraint on the Jacobian altogether.
