nde.lead: A residual block computes $h_{t+1} = h_t + f(h_t)$, which is an Euler step of a differential equation with unit step size. Neural ODEs take that reading seriously: replace the stack of layers with a single learned vector field, integrate it with an off-the-shelf solver, and let the solver decide how many steps the problem needs.

blocks.b:
Instead of a finite sequence of transformations, define the hidden state's evolution:

$$\frac{d\mathbf{h}(t)}{dt} = f\big(\mathbf{h}(t), t, \theta\big)$$

and obtain the output by integrating from $t_0$ to $t_1$. The network $f$ is shared across all of $t$ — one set of weights, not one per layer — and the number of function evaluations is chosen by the solver according to a requested error tolerance rather than fixed by the architecture.

This makes accuracy a runtime parameter. A trained model can be evaluated more cheaply and less exactly, or more expensively and more precisely, without retraining, which no discrete stack permits.

Backpropagating through a solver by storing every intermediate step costs memory proportional to the number of steps, which defeats the purpose. The adjoint sensitivity method avoids it: define $\mathbf{a}(t) = \partial L / \partial \mathbf{h}(t)$ and integrate it **backwards** in time,

$$\frac{d\mathbf{a}(t)}{dt} = -\mathbf{a}(t)^{\top} \frac{\partial f(\mathbf{h}(t), t, \theta)}{\partial \mathbf{h}}$$

alongside the state itself, accumulating the parameter gradient as a third integral. Memory is $O(1)$ in the number of steps, because nothing is stored — the forward trajectory is reconstructed by running the dynamics in reverse.

The catch is that reversing the ODE is not numerically free. Error accumulates, and for stiff systems the reconstructed trajectory drifts from the original, which is why later work often reverts to checkpointing part of the path.

The generative payoff is a change to the change-of-variables formula. For a discrete invertible layer one needs a log-determinant; in continuous time the density evolves by

$$\frac{\partial \log p(\mathbf{z}(t))}{\partial t} = -\mathrm{tr}\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial \mathbf{z}(t)}\right)$$

A **trace** rather than a determinant. That is a large structural gain: a determinant is only cheap for triangular or otherwise constrained Jacobians, which is why NICE, RealNVP and Glow all had to engineer their architectures around it. A trace is linear, so the constraint on $f$ disappears — any vector field will do, and the coupling layers can be dropped entirely.

Invertibility also comes free rather than by construction: an ODE with a Lipschitz vector field has a unique solution in both directions, so the map is a bijection whatever $f$ is.

blocks.h: The solver becomes the cost model
blocks.b:
Trading a fixed layer count for an adaptive solver means the cost of a forward pass is no longer known in advance, and it grows during training — as the learned dynamics become stiffer, the solver takes more steps for the same tolerance, so later epochs are slower than earlier ones with no change to the model's size.

Computing the exact trace still costs $D$ backward passes for a $D$-dimensional state, so the constraint has moved rather than vanished; FFJORD's Hutchinson estimator is what removes it. And a first-order ODE cannot cross its own trajectories, which restricts the class of homeomorphisms representable — the augmented variants add dimensions to work around it.

The more lasting influence is on how the field thinks about generative transport. Once generation is an ODE from noise to data, the question becomes what path to take, and flow matching and rectified flow are answers to exactly that.

Augmented Neural ODEs

ffjord.lead: Neural ODEs replaced the flow's log-determinant with a trace, which removes the need for a constrained Jacobian in principle. Computing that trace exactly still costs one backward pass per dimension. FFJORD estimates it stochastically instead, and the flow becomes genuinely free-form — any architecture, no structural constraint at all.

blocks.b:
For any square matrix $A$ and any random vector $\epsilon$ with zero mean and unit covariance,

$$\mathrm{tr}(A) = \mathbb{E}_{p(\epsilon)}\big[\epsilon^{\top} A \, \epsilon\big]$$

Applied to the Jacobian, $\epsilon^{\top} (\partial f / \partial \mathbf{z})$ is a vector-Jacobian product, which is exactly what reverse-mode automatic differentiation computes in a single backward pass. So an unbiased estimate of the trace costs one pass rather than $D$.

The estimator is noisy, but the noise enters an expectation that is already being estimated by sampling over data and over time, and a single $\epsilon$ per solver step suffices in practice. The same $\epsilon$ is held fixed along a trajectory, which the paper notes keeps the estimated dynamics consistent.

With the trace cheap, nothing constrains $f$. There is no coupling layer, no masking pattern, no requirement that the Jacobian be triangular, no fixed permutation between layers, and no split of the input into a transformed and an untransformed half.

That matters because every earlier flow spent its design budget on the determinant. NICE gave up scaling; RealNVP left half the input untouched per layer; Glow needed a learned $1\times1$ convolution to mix channels because its coupling could not. FFJORD needs none of it — the vector field can be an ordinary convolutional network — and it reported the best density estimates among flows of its moment on standard image benchmarks, with a single continuous transformation replacing a deep stack of restricted ones.

blocks.h: Reversible in both directions, one model
blocks.b:
The construction retains the flow family's defining property in a cleaner form. Integrating the ODE forwards maps data to noise and gives an exact log-likelihood; integrating backwards maps noise to data and gives a sample. One network, run in two directions, no approximation in either.

Unlike the discrete flows the model also has no architectural asymmetry between the directions — MAF and IAF differ in which direction is parallel, and FFJORD has no such distinction, since both are solver integrations of the same field.

The cost is now entirely the adaptive solver's, and it is unpredictable. Function evaluations per forward pass grow as training makes the learned dynamics stiffer, so the same model gets slower over a run, and the number is not known in advance for any given input.

Regularising for straighter trajectories helps — later work penalises the kinetic energy or the Jacobian norm of the field explicitly to keep the ODE easy to solve — and that observation is the direct ancestor of what came next. If the difficulty is that the learned path is curved, then specify a straight path in advance and regress the field onto it: no simulation during training, and few solver steps at sampling time. Flow matching and rectified flow are that idea, and they make FFJORD's adaptive-solver cost the problem to be designed away.

Neural Ordinary Differential Equations

rectflow.lead: If generation is transport from noise to data along an ODE, the natural question is which path to take, and the cheapest path to integrate is a straight line. Rectified flow learns the field that follows straight interpolations between the two distributions, then applies a procedure that straightens it further — until a single Euler step is enough.

blocks.b:
Take $X_0$ from the noise distribution and $X_1$ from the data, pair them arbitrarily, and define the linear interpolation $X_t = (1-t) X_0 + t X_1$. Its velocity is constant along the path and equal to $X_1 - X_0$. Train a field to match it:

$$\min_{v} \; \mathbb{E}_{X_0, X_1, t}\Big[\big\| (X_1 - X_0) - v(X_t, t) \big\|^2\Big]$$

This is a plain regression. No simulation of the ODE during training, no divergence or trace to compute, no adversary, no bound — the whole objective is a squared error against a target that is available in closed form.

The learned field cannot follow the straight lines exactly, because many interpolation paths cross the same point with different velocities and the regression returns their average. What it does produce is a valid ODE whose marginals match the interpolation's, which is enough for the endpoints to be right.

The averaging is what makes the trajectories curved, and it is also what makes them improvable. Solving the learned ODE gives a **coupling** — each noise sample now maps to a specific data sample rather than an arbitrary one — and re-running the training on that coupling gives paths that cross far less.

Repeating this **reflow** procedure straightens the field progressively, and the paper's key property is that it never increases the transport cost: the coupling improves or stays the same at each round. Once trajectories are nearly straight, the ODE can be integrated with very few Euler steps, and in the limit a single step suffices — one network evaluation for a sample, against the hundreds a diffusion model needs.

Distillation can then be applied on top of the straightened model for the final one-step form, which is cheap precisely because the teacher's paths are already close to linear.

blocks.h: The same idea as flow matching
blocks.b:
Rectified flow, flow matching and stochastic interpolants appeared within months of each other and arrive at the same construction from different starting points — an ODE trained by regressing a velocity onto a prescribed interpolation path, with no simulation in the loop.

What rectified flow adds is the emphasis on straightness as an explicit objective and the reflow procedure that pursues it. What flow matching adds is the general conditional formulation showing that diffusion's path is one choice among many. In practice the linear-interpolation schedule is what large systems adopted, and Stable Diffusion 3's rectified-flow objective on a DiT backbone is the direct application.

blocks.h: The straightness has to be paid for
blocks.b:
Reflow is not free: each round requires generating a full synthetic dataset by solving the ODE, then retraining. So the one-step model is bought with several multiples of the original training cost, and it is a distillation pipeline rather than a single training run.

Each round also compounds on the previous model's errors, since the coupling it trains on is produced by an imperfect field, and quality can degrade as straightness improves. The usual practice is one or two reflow rounds rather than many.

In this graph the node stands alone — no lineage edge connects it, though its natural neighbours are flow matching, which shares its formulation, and the diffusion line it competes with on sampling cost.

Building Normalizing Flows with Stochastic Interpolants

flowmatch.lead: Continuous normalising flows had the right shape and an impossible training cost — every gradient step required solving an ODE. Flow matching removes the simulation entirely by regressing the vector field onto a target that can be written down in closed form, and in doing so reveals diffusion as one particular choice of path among many.

blocks.h: Why the obvious objective is intractable
blocks.b:
Given a probability path $p_t$ interpolating noise and data, the field generating it satisfies a continuity equation, and one could regress onto it:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t, p_t(x)} \big\| v_\theta(t, x) - u_t(x) \big\|^2$$

This is useless as written, because neither the marginal path $p_t$ nor its field $u_t$ has a closed form — both are marginals over the whole dataset.

The paper's central result is that conditioning on a single data point fixes this. Define the path **per example**, $p_t(x \mid x_1)$, which is a simple Gaussian one can write down, and regress onto its field:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t, q(x_1), p_t(x \mid x_1)} \big\| v_\theta(t, x) - u_t(x \mid x_1) \big\|^2$$

The two losses have **identical gradients** with respect to $\theta$. So optimising the tractable conditional objective optimises the intractable marginal one, and nothing is approximated.

Everything in the conditional objective is available: sample a data point, sample a time, sample a point on that example's path, evaluate the target velocity analytically. No ODE is solved during training, no divergence is estimated, and the whole thing is a regression — the same practical profile as diffusion's noise-prediction objective.

blocks.h: Diffusion is one path among many
blocks.b:
With the framework in place, the probability path becomes a design choice. Choosing the Gaussian path implied by a variance-preserving diffusion recovers score-based training as a special case — flow matching contains it.

Choosing instead the **optimal transport** path, whose conditional interpolation is a straight line with constant velocity, gives something better behaved. Diffusion's path curves and its velocity varies along $t$; the linear path does not, and the paper shows it trains faster, generalises better, and — because the trajectories are close to straight — needs markedly fewer solver steps at sampling time.

That is the practical headline: sample quality comparable to diffusion at a fraction of the function evaluations, from a change of interpolation schedule rather than a change of architecture.

blocks.h: What it did and did not settle
blocks.b:
Flow matching became the default objective for large generative systems within about two years. Stable Diffusion 3 trains a DiT with a rectified-flow objective, and the video and audio models that followed use the same formulation, with the older $\epsilon$-prediction diffusion loss increasingly treated as the special case it is.

What remains open is the pairing. The conditional construction pairs each data point with independently drawn noise, so the induced coupling is arbitrary and the marginal field still averages over crossing paths — which is why trajectories are straighter than diffusion's but not straight. Rectified flow's reflow procedure and the minibatch optimal-transport variants attack exactly this, at the cost of extra training rounds. And the framework says nothing about what makes a good path beyond the two it compares, so the choice of schedule remains empirical.

Flow Straight and Fast: Learning to Generate and Transfer Data with Rectified Flow

ncsn.lead: Every likelihood-based model must contend with the normalising constant, and every energy-based model with sampling from an unnormalised density. Score matching sidesteps both by learning the gradient of the log-density rather than the density — the constant differentiates away — and Langevin dynamics turns that gradient into a sampler.

blocks.h: The score, and why it is easier
blocks.b:
The score is $\nabla_x \log p(x)$, a vector field pointing towards higher density. Writing $p(x) = \tilde{p}(x)/Z$, the intractable $Z$ vanishes under the gradient because $\log Z$ is constant in $x$. So a model of the score need never represent or estimate the partition function.

Given a score, Langevin dynamics generates samples by following it with noise added:

$$x_{t+1} = x_t + \frac{\epsilon}{2} \nabla_x \log p(x_t) + \sqrt{\epsilon}\, z_t, \qquad z_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$$

which converges to $p$ as $\epsilon \to 0$ and the number of steps grows. Training uses denoising score matching, which is equivalent to predicting the noise added to a perturbed sample — a plain regression, with no adversary and no bound.

Song and Ermon's contribution is diagnosing why the naive version does not work on images.

First, the **manifold problem**. Natural images occupy a low-dimensional manifold in pixel space, so $\nabla_x \log p(x)$ is undefined off it — and almost every point is off it. The score estimate is therefore trained nowhere near where a sampler initialised from noise begins.

Second, **low-density regions**. Score matching's objective is weighted by the data density, so regions with few samples get almost no training signal. Langevin dynamics starting from noise spends its early steps precisely in those regions, following a score the model never learned. And when the distribution has separated modes, Langevin mixing between them is slow enough to be useless, so the relative weight of the modes comes out wrong.

blocks.h: Perturb at many scales, then anneal
blocks.b:
Both failures have the same fix: add Gaussian noise. A noised distribution has support everywhere, so the score is defined everywhere, and enough noise makes the density high in regions that were empty.

But large noise destroys the fine structure one wants to sample. So NCSN uses a **geometric sequence** of noise levels $\sigma_1 > \cdots > \sigma_L$ and trains a single network conditioned on the level to estimate the score of each perturbed distribution at once, with the loss weighted so all levels contribute comparably.

Sampling then runs **annealed Langevin dynamics**: start at the largest noise level, run a few steps, use the result to initialise the next level down, and continue. Early levels place the sample in roughly the right mode, where the score is well-estimated at any scale; later levels refine detail. The samples were competitive with GANs on CIFAR-10, from a stable regression objective with no adversary.

Read from a distance, this is the same procedure DDPM arrives at from a variational starting point a year later: a single network conditioned on a noise level, trained to predict noise, sampled by walking from most-noisy to least. The two lines were formally unified by the score-SDE framework, which shows NCSN and DDPM as the variance-exploding and variance-preserving discretisations of one stochastic differential equation.

What NCSN left unresolved is cost and tuning. Annealed Langevin needs many steps at every level, so sampling is slow, and the noise schedule, the step sizes and the number of steps per level are all hand-set — the paper's follow-up is largely about choosing them. DDPM's contribution on this axis is a simpler objective and a cleaner schedule; DDIM's is removing most of the steps.

ddpm.lead: Diffusion models had been proposed in 2015 and produced nothing competitive. DDPM's contribution is not the framework but the simplification: a specific parameterisation in which the variational bound reduces to predicting the noise added to an image with plain squared error, at which point the models became the best in the field.

blocks.h: The forward process, and the property that matters
blocks.b:
The forward process destroys an image by adding Gaussian noise over $T$ steps according to a fixed schedule $\beta_1, \ldots, \beta_T$. It has no parameters and nothing is learned about it.

Its crucial property is that the composition of many Gaussian steps is Gaussian, so any intermediate step is available in closed form. With $\alpha_t = 1 - \beta_t$ and $\bar{\alpha}_t = \prod_{s \le t} \alpha_s$,

$$q(x_t \mid x_0) = \mathcal{N}\big(x_t; \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}\, x_0, \; (1 - \bar{\alpha}_t) I\big)$$

Training can therefore jump straight to a random timestep — sample $t$, sample noise, form $x_t$ in one operation — rather than simulating the chain. That is what makes the objective cheap, and it is the same structural advantage flow matching later exploits for ODE paths.

The reverse process is learned, and the variational bound decomposes into KL terms between Gaussians, each of which has a closed form. Ho et al. then observe that reparameterising the mean in terms of the noise, and dropping the weighting the bound prescribes, gives

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{simple}} = \mathbb{E}_{t, x_0, \epsilon}\Big[\big\| \epsilon - \epsilon_\theta\big(\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}\, x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}\, \epsilon,\; t\big) \big\|^2\Big]$$

Predict the noise. That is the entire training procedure: one network, one squared error, no adversary, no bound to balance, no discriminator to keep in step, and a loss that decreases monotonically and means something.

The paper notes that this reweighting is not the bound — it down-weights the small-$t$ terms — and that it produces better samples anyway. It also connects the parameterisation directly to denoising score matching: $\epsilon_\theta$ is, up to scaling, the score of the noised distribution, which is why DDPM and NCSN converge on the same algorithm from different derivations.

The denoiser is a U-Net, taken from segmentation with three changes: the timestep is embedded sinusoidally and injected into every residual block so one network serves all noise levels; self-attention blocks are added at the lower resolutions where the token count is affordable; and group normalisation replaces batch normalisation, since sampling has no batch statistics.

The reverse variances are fixed to schedule constants rather than learned, which the paper finds works as well as learning them and removes a source of instability. This architecture held for years — improved and scaled, moved into a latent space by Stable Diffusion, but structurally unchanged until DiT replaced it with a transformer.

The cost is at sampling time and it is severe. The reverse process is Markovian, so producing one image requires $T$ sequential network evaluations, with $T = 1000$ in the paper. Against a GAN's single forward pass that is three orders of magnitude, and it is the reason diffusion was initially regarded as impractical despite its sample quality.

Everything downstream in this lane is a response. DDIM constructs a non-Markovian process with the same marginals that can be sampled in tens of steps. Latent diffusion moves the process into a compressed space so each step is cheaper. Distillation and consistency models compress the trajectory into a handful of steps, and rectified flow into one. The stability DDPM bought — a stationary regression objective, no adversary, no collapse — turned out to be worth paying for, and the rest of the field's work has been on reducing the bill.

Improved Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models

scoresde.lead: NCSN and DDPM were developed from different premises — score matching with Langevin dynamics on one side, a variational bound on a Markov chain on the other — and arrived at nearly the same algorithm. Score SDE shows why: both are discretisations of one stochastic differential equation, differing only in which.

blocks.b:
Write the noising process in continuous time:

$$d\mathbf{x} = f(\mathbf{x}, t)\, dt + g(t)\, d\mathbf{w}$$

with $\mathbf{w}$ a Wiener process. Two choices of $f$ and $g$ recover the two known models. Setting $f = 0$ and letting $g$ grow gives the **variance exploding** SDE, whose discretisation is NCSN's sequence of increasing noise scales. Setting $f = -\tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\mathbf{x}$ with $g = \sqrt{\beta(t)}$ gives the **variance preserving** SDE, whose discretisation is DDPM's forward chain.

So the two lines are not competing methods but neighbouring points in one family, and the continuous view makes the noise schedule a function to be designed rather than a list of constants to be tuned. The paper introduces a third, sub-VP, that improves likelihoods.

blocks.h: The reverse SDE and the score
blocks.b:
Anderson's result gives the time reversal of any such process:

$$d\mathbf{x} = \big[f(\mathbf{x}, t) - g(t)^2 \nabla_{\mathbf{x}} \log p_t(\mathbf{x})\big] dt + g(t)\, d\bar{\mathbf{w}}$$

The only unknown is the score of the noised marginal, which is exactly what a denoising network estimates. Generation is therefore integrating this reverse SDE with a learned score in place of the true one, and every diffusion sampler is a numerical scheme for it — which turns sampler design into a solver question with a century of numerical analysis behind it.

**Predictor-corrector** sampling follows from that reading: alternate a step of a standard SDE solver with a few Langevin corrector steps that use only the score, so numerical error introduced by the predictor is repaired before it accumulates.

The more consequential result is that there is a deterministic process with the **same marginals at every time**:

$$d\mathbf{x} = \Big[f(\mathbf{x}, t) - \tfrac{1}{2} g(t)^2 \nabla_{\mathbf{x}} \log p_t(\mathbf{x})\Big] dt$$

No noise term. This makes a diffusion model a continuous normalising flow, which brings three things at once: exact likelihood computation via the instantaneous change-of-variables formula, a uniquely identifiable latent for any image so that encoding and interpolation become well-defined, and access to fast black-box ODE solvers.

DDIM's deterministic sampler is a particular discretisation of this ODE, so the two papers meet here. And once generation is an ODE from noise to data, the question of which path to take becomes explicit — which is where flow matching and rectified flow begin.

blocks.h: What it unified, and what it left
blocks.b:
The framework is why the field stopped distinguishing score-based and diffusion models. It supplied controllable generation — inpainting, colourisation and class-conditional sampling as modifications to the reverse SDE — and competitive likelihoods for a family that had not previously offered any.

It does not make sampling cheap. The reverse SDE still needs many steps to integrate accurately, and the paper's own high-quality results use substantial step counts; predictor-corrector improves quality per step rather than removing the requirement. Score estimates are also worst in exactly the low-density regions the trajectory passes through early, so error compounds where the model is least reliable. Reducing the step count is the work of DDIM, distillation, consistency models and the straight-path flows, all of which take this ODE as their starting point.

refs.t: Score-Based Generative Modeling through Stochastic Differential Equations
Reverse-time diffusion equation models

ddim.lead: DDPM's reverse process is Markovian, so a thousand training steps means a thousand sampling steps. DDIM's observation is that the training objective depends only on the marginals $q(x_t \mid x_0)$, not on the joint — so one can construct a different, non-Markovian process with the same marginals, and sample it in a fraction of the steps with no retraining.

blocks.h: The objective does not pin down the process
blocks.b:
DDPM's simplified loss trains a network to predict the noise in $x_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\, x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\, \epsilon$. Every term refers to a single marginal; nothing in it constrains how consecutive timesteps relate.

DDIM constructs a family of forward processes, indexed by a parameter $\sigma$, that share those marginals but are not Markov chains — each step conditions on $x_0$ as well as on the previous state. Any trained DDPM is therefore already a valid model for every member of the family, and the choice can be made at sampling time.

Setting $\sigma = 0$ makes the reverse process fully deterministic. Given the latent, the output is fixed, and the model becomes an implicit map from noise to image rather than a stochastic chain — which is the origin of the name.

The practical consequence is that sampling need not visit every timestep. Because the process is defined by marginals, a subsequence $\tau_1 < \cdots < \tau_S$ of the original $T$ steps defines a valid shorter process, and the update from $x_{\tau_i}$ to $x_{\tau_{i-1}}$ is

$$x_{\tau_{i-1}} = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_{\tau_{i-1}}}\; \underbrace{\left(\frac{x_{\tau_i} - \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_{\tau_i}}\; \epsilon_\theta(x_{\tau_i})}{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{\tau_i}}}\right)}_{\text{predicted } x_0} + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_{\tau_{i-1}}}\; \epsilon_\theta(x_{\tau_i})$$

Each step predicts $x_0$ from the current state and then re-noises it to the next level down. Twenty to fifty steps produce samples close to the thousand-step DDPM, a speedup of one to two orders of magnitude from a change of sampler alone.

Determinism gives the model something DDPM lacks: a meaningful latent. The same noise vector always produces the same image, so interpolating between two latents produces a smooth semantic transition rather than two unrelated samples — the property GAN latent spaces were valued for.

The deterministic sampler can also be run backwards to encode a real image into its latent, approximately, which is what image editing and inversion methods in diffusion are built on.

The paper also notes that samples generated from the same latent with different step counts are similar in high-level content, so the latent encodes the image and the step count trades detail — one can preview cheaply and then render the same image properly.

blocks.h: Fidelity is still bought with steps
blocks.b:
The trade is manual and real. Fewer steps means larger integration error, which shows as lost fine detail and slightly degraded FID, and the acceptable floor varies by model and by dataset. Nothing in DDIM tells you where to stop.

The deterministic sampler was later understood as a first-order discretisation of the probability-flow ODE, which is what opened the door to better solvers — DPM-Solver and its relatives use higher-order schemes tailored to the semi-linear structure and reach comparable quality in ten steps or fewer. Beyond that, the step count is reduced not by better integration but by changing the model: distillation, consistency models, and the straight-path flows that make a single Euler step sufficient.

ldm.lead: Diffusion in pixel space spends most of its capacity and nearly all of its compute on imperceptible high-frequency detail. Latent diffusion trains an autoencoder first, throws away exactly that detail, and runs the diffusion process in the compressed space — which is what made text-to-image generation cheap enough to release.

blocks.h: Two stages, and where to cut between them
blocks.b:
The first stage is an autoencoder trained with a perceptual loss and a patch-based adversarial term, compressing an image by a factor $f$ per side — $f = 4$ or $8$ in the released models. The adversarial term matters: a plain reconstruction loss gives blurry decodings, and the discriminator is what keeps the decoder sharp at high compression.

The second stage is an ordinary diffusion model over that latent. At $f = 8$ a $512 \times 512$ image becomes a $64 \times 64$ latent, so each denoising step costs roughly sixty-four times less.

The paper frames the split as separating **perceptual** compression from **semantic** compression. The autoencoder removes detail the eye does not attend to; the diffusion model then works in a space where almost every dimension carries meaning, which is a far better use of its capacity. Choosing $f$ is a genuine trade — too little and the saving is small, too much and the autoencoder becomes the quality ceiling.

The second contribution is general conditioning. A domain-specific encoder $\tau_\theta$ maps the condition — text, a segmentation map, a layout — to a sequence, and the U-Net's intermediate features attend to it:

$$\mathrm{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d}}\right)V, \qquad Q = W_Q \varphi(z_t), \; K = W_K \tau_\theta(y), \; V = W_V \tau_\theta(y)$$

Cross-attention layers are inserted throughout the U-Net, so conditioning acts at every resolution rather than being concatenated once at the input. Because the interface is a sequence of embeddings, any modality with an encoder can be plugged in without changing the diffusion model — and in Stable Diffusion the text encoder is CLIP's, frozen.

Combined with classifier-free guidance, which extrapolates away from the unconditional prediction to make the condition bite harder, this is the arrangement essentially every text-to-image system used for the next several years.

The compute reduction is what turned a research result into infrastructure. Stable Diffusion runs inference on consumer hardware, and fine-tuning it is within reach of an individual — which is why the ecosystem around it, LoRA adapters, ControlNet, textual inversion, DreamBooth, grew as it did and largely did not around the closed models of the same period.

The weights being public is a separate fact from the architecture, but the two are connected: a model that needed a datacentre to sample would not have produced that ecosystem regardless of licence.

No amount of diffusion quality recovers what the first stage discarded. Small text, fine regular textures and precise faces are the standing failure cases, and they are reconstruction failures rather than generation failures — encoding and decoding a real image exhibits them without any diffusion at all.

The two stages are also trained separately, so nothing optimises the latent space for being easy to model. And the system inherits diffusion's sampling cost, reduced by the compression but not removed; the U-Net backbone likewise carries its own hand-tuned structure, which is what DiT replaced with a transformer whose quality scales predictably with compute.

dit.lead: Diffusion models had inherited the U-Net from DDPM and kept it, tuned by hand, with no relationship between its size and its output quality. DiT replaces it with a plain Vision Transformer over latent patches and demonstrates the property the U-Net never had: sample quality that improves predictably as compute is added.

blocks.b:
Operating on a VAE latent, DiT patchifies it into tokens, adds positional embeddings, and runs a standard transformer stack — no downsampling, no skip connections, no convolution anywhere.

The patch size $p$ is the interesting parameter. Halving it quadruples the token count and therefore the FLOPs, at **unchanged** parameter count. The paper's central measurement is that FID tracks total FLOPs rather than parameters: a smaller model at $p = 2$ beats a larger one at $p = 8$. Model size and patch size are two routes to the same currency, and it is the currency that predicts quality.

That is a scaling law of the kind language modelling had and image generation did not, and it converts architecture design into a budget decision.

Conditioning on the timestep and class label is where the design work sits, and the paper compares four options: in-context tokens, cross-attention, adaptive layer normalisation, and a zero-initialised variant of the last.

Adaptive LayerNorm regresses each normalisation's scale and shift from the conditioning vector. **adaLN-Zero** additionally regresses a gate $\alpha$ on each residual branch and initialises the layer producing it to zero:

$$x \leftarrow x + \alpha \cdot \mathrm{Attention}\big(\gamma \cdot \mathrm{LN}(x) + \beta\big)$$

so every block starts as the exact identity and grows its contribution only as training finds a use for it. This is the residual-scaling idea Inception-ResNet needed for stability, made learned and per-block. It is both the best-performing option in the ablation and the cheapest, since conditioning enters through normalisation parameters rather than through extra attention layers.

DiT set the state of the art on class-conditional ImageNet generation, and more consequentially it settled the backbone question. Stable Diffusion 3 is a transformer; the large video models are transformers; Sora's spacetime patches are DiT's construction extended over time. The U-Net's decade as the default denoiser ends here.

The reason is not only quality. A transformer inherits the whole engineering stack built for language models — sharding, kernel fusion, sequence parallelism, established scaling behaviour — none of which transfers to a bespoke convolutional architecture with attention at chosen resolutions.

Attention is quadratic in token count, so fine patch sizes are expensive and the design depends on the latent being small — DiT is not a pixel-space model and there is no version of it that is affordable at full resolution.

Training is also slower to converge than a U-Net at equal compute, which is the usual price for removing an inductive bias, and it is only worth paying because the scaling behaviour makes additional compute reliably useful. The model inherits the two-stage structure's ceiling as well: whatever the VAE discarded is not recoverable, however large the transformer.

sd3.lead: Stable Diffusion 3 is where the two threads of this lane's recent work meet in a shipped system: rectified flow as the training objective in place of the diffusion loss, and a transformer backbone in which text and image tokens are processed by separate weights while attending to each other.

blocks.h: Rectified flow, with the schedule studied
blocks.b:
Training regresses a velocity field onto straight interpolations between noise and data rather than predicting noise under a diffusion schedule. The paper's contribution is not the objective but a systematic comparison: it evaluates a range of diffusion and flow formulations under matched conditions and finds the rectified-flow variants ahead.

The detail that mattered is timestep sampling. A uniform distribution over $t$ spends equal effort everywhere, and the middle of the trajectory is where the prediction problem is hardest. SD3 samples $t$ from a logit-normal distribution, concentrating training there, and reports a clear gain.

Resolution needs a further correction. A larger image carries more redundancy, so a given noise level destroys proportionally less information, and the schedule has to be **shifted** towards higher noise as resolution rises for the difficulty to stay matched.

The backbone is a DiT with one structural change. Text and image tokens are different kinds of object, and forcing them through shared weights makes one modality's statistics interfere with the other's. **MMDiT** gives each modality its own projections, its own normalisation parameters and its own feed-forward block — two parameter sets in each layer — while the attention operation runs over the concatenated sequence so the two interact fully.

So the mixing happens in attention, where it should, and the per-modality processing stays separate. The paper's ablation shows this beating both a shared-weight transformer and cross-attention conditioning.

Three text encoders are used together — two CLIP models and T5-XXL — with the T5 branch optional at inference, trading typography and prompt adherence for memory. That the large language-model encoder is what supplies detailed text understanding is the same finding Imagen reported.

blocks.h: What it fixed at the application level
blocks.b:
Two long-standing failures improve markedly. Rendering legible text inside an image had been a reliable weakness of the whole family; SD3 handles short strings substantially better, which the paper attributes to the T5 encoder and the MMDiT arrangement. Prompts specifying multiple subjects with distinct attributes — the binding problem, where a red cube and a blue sphere become two objects of confused colour — also improve.

Both are conditioning failures rather than generation failures, which is consistent with where the architectural work went.

Straight-path training reduces the number of sampling steps but does not remove the need for several; a single-step model requires the reflow or distillation rounds that rectified flow's own paper describes, at extra training cost.

The two-stage structure and its autoencoder ceiling remain, as does the dependence on very large text encoders — T5-XXL is a substantial fraction of the deployed system's memory. And the model is large enough to train that the released weights, rather than the recipe, are what most people can use; the paper is a description of an industrial system as much as a method.
